meta.description: Chapter-by-chapter curriculum for FinanceLab. PDF page = book page + 36. Each session is ~30 min. Chapters marked difficulty: 1 (easy) to 3 (hard).

sessions.title: The Language of Business & the IFRS Framework
learningObjectives: Explain why accounting is called the 'language of business' and who uses financial reports
Distinguish between financial accounting and management accounting
Identify the four main forms of business organization (proprietorship, partnership, company, LLP)
Describe the IFRS Conceptual Framework: qualitative characteristics (relevance, faithful representation, comparability, verifiability, timeliness, understandability)
State the key accounting assumptions: going concern, accrual basis, monetary unit, time period
Explain the role of IASB and why global accounting standards matter
keyConcepts: Financial accounting vs. management accounting
IFRS vs. GAAP — why IFRS matters for European/global companies
Qualitative characteristics of useful financial information
Going concern assumption
Accrual basis of accounting
The accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
coreFormulasForLibrary: Assets = Liabilities + Equity (the fundamental accounting equation)
Equity = Assets − Liabilities
Net Income = Revenues − Expenses
quizTopics: Multiple choice: identify which qualitative characteristic applies in a given scenario
Short answer: explain the difference between financial and management accounting
Short answer: why does the going concern assumption matter for how we value assets?
sessions.analystNote: Every PE/IB interview starts with the accounting equation. Know it cold and be able to explain what happens to equity when each line item changes.

sessions.title: The Four Financial Statements & How They Connect
learningObjectives: Identify and describe the four financial statements: Income Statement, Statement of Changes in Equity, Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position), Statement of Cash Flows
Explain what each statement shows and the time period it covers (period vs. point in time)
Trace how the statements link: net income flows into equity; ending cash on SCF ties to balance sheet cash
Read a simple set of financial statements for a real company (Alibaba)
Understand the role of ethics and the IESBA Code of Ethics in accounting
keyConcepts: Income Statement: revenues, expenses, net income/loss — covers a period
Statement of Changes in Equity: opening equity + net income − dividends = closing equity
Balance Sheet: snapshot at a point in time — assets, liabilities, equity
Statement of Cash Flows: operating, investing, financing activities
The articulation of the four statements (how they link together)
Retained earnings as the link between income statement and balance sheet
coreFormulasForLibrary: Ending Retained Earnings = Beginning Retained Earnings + Net Income − Dividends
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
The four financial statements: IS → SCE → BS → SCF (order of preparation)
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given revenue and expense figures, complete a simple income statement and trace net income to the equity statement
Multiple choice: which statement would you look at to assess a company's liquidity?
Short answer: explain in your own words how the four statements are interconnected
sessions.analystNote: Interviewers will ask you to 'walk me through the financial statements.' Practice narrating all four in under 90 seconds, explaining how they connect.

sessions.title: The Accounting System: Accounts, Debits & Credits
learningObjectives: Define a business transaction and explain what makes an event recordable
Identify assets, liabilities, and equity accounts and their normal balances
Explain the T-account structure and the rules of debit and credit (DEAD CLIC mnemonic)
Understand double-entry accounting: every transaction affects at least two accounts
Journalize basic transactions using proper journal entry format
Post journal entries to T-accounts (the ledger)
keyConcepts: Chart of accounts
T-account: left side = debit, right side = credit
Normal balances: Assets & Expenses debit; Liabilities, Equity & Revenue credit
Double-entry bookkeeping: debits always equal credits
Journal entry format: date, accounts debited/credited, amounts
Posting: transferring journal entries to the ledger
coreFormulasForLibrary: Debit = Left side of T-account; Credit = Right side of T-account
Normal balance rule: Assets/Expenses → Debit normal; Liabilities/Equity/Revenue → Credit normal
Double-entry rule: Total Debits = Total Credits for every transaction
quizTopics: Multiple choice: which accounts are debited/credited in a given transaction?
Fill-in-the-blank: complete a journal entry for a purchase of equipment on credit
Short answer: explain why double-entry accounting matters for the integrity of financial statements
sessions.analystNote: You won't be journalizing in PE, but understanding debits/credits lets you instantly see how any transaction hits all three statements — a skill analysts use daily.

sessions.title: Trial Balance & Analyzing Transactions
learningObjectives: Construct a trial balance and explain its purpose
Identify and correct basic accounting errors using the trial balance
Analyze a series of transactions using only T-accounts (without formal journal entries)
Understand account formats and the chart of accounts structure
Read and interpret a simple ledger to reconstruct what happened in a period
keyConcepts: Trial balance: list of all accounts with debit/credit balances — must balance
Limitations of the trial balance (doesn't catch all errors)
Transposition errors vs. slide errors
The normal balance of each account type
Using T-accounts to analyze the flow of money through a business
coreFormulasForLibrary: Trial Balance check: Sum of all Debit balances = Sum of all Credit balances
To find a missing figure: plug the account balance using the accounting equation
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank financial statement: given a set of T-accounts, construct the trial balance
Multiple choice: identify which error would NOT be caught by a trial balance
Short answer: walk through three transactions for a startup company using T-accounts
sessions.analystNote: Trial balance skills translate directly to building 3-statement models — you're essentially making sure your model 'balances' just like a trial balance does.

sessions.title: Accrual vs. Cash Basis & Adjusting Entries
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between accrual accounting and cash-basis accounting with real examples
Apply the revenue recognition principle (IFRS 15): revenue recognized when performance obligation satisfied
Apply the expense recognition/matching principle: expenses matched to the revenues they generate
Identify the four categories of adjusting entries: prepaid expenses, unearned revenues, accrued expenses, accrued revenues
Prepare adjusting journal entries for each category
Explain why Richemont could have high profits but declining cash (accruals vs. cash)
keyConcepts: Accrual basis: record revenue when earned, expenses when incurred — regardless of cash
Revenue recognition principle (IFRS 15)
Matching principle (expense recognition)
Prepaid expenses: asset that gets expensed over time (e.g. prepaid rent)
Unearned revenues: liability until service is delivered
Accrued expenses: expense incurred but not yet paid (e.g. wages payable)
Accrued revenues: revenue earned but not yet received (e.g. interest receivable)
coreFormulasForLibrary: Adjusting entry for prepaid: Dr. Expense / Cr. Prepaid Asset
Adjusting entry for unearned revenue: Dr. Unearned Revenue / Cr. Revenue
Adjusting entry for accrued expense: Dr. Expense / Cr. Payable
Adjusting entry for accrued revenue: Dr. Receivable / Cr. Revenue
quizTopics: Multiple choice: classify each scenario into one of the four adjusting entry types
Fill-in-the-blank: complete the adjusting entry for a company that received 12-month rent in advance
Short answer: explain why a company can show a profit but run out of cash
sessions.analystNote: Accruals are why EBITDA and cash flow differ. In LBO models, changes in working capital (accruals) are a major driver of free cash flow. Understanding this is fundamental.

sessions.title: Adjusted Trial Balance, Closing Entries & Financial Statements
learningObjectives: Prepare an adjusted trial balance after recording all adjusting entries
Prepare financial statements directly from the adjusted trial balance
Understand closing entries: why temporary accounts (revenues, expenses, dividends) are closed to retained earnings
Distinguish between temporary accounts (closed each period) and permanent accounts (carried forward)
Compute and interpret the current ratio as a measure of short-term liquidity
keyConcepts: Adjusted trial balance: trial balance after all adjusting entries posted
The accounting cycle: journal → post → adjust → financial statements → close
Closing entries: zero out income statement accounts, transfer net income to retained earnings
Temporary accounts: revenues, expenses, dividends
Permanent accounts: assets, liabilities, equity (carry forward)
Current ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
coreFormulasForLibrary: Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities (measures short-term liquidity)
Post-closing retained earnings = Pre-closing RE + Net Income − Dividends
Accounting cycle order: Analyze → Journalize → Post → Adjust → Financial Statements → Close
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given an adjusted trial balance, prepare the income statement and balance sheet
Multiple choice: which accounts appear on the post-closing trial balance?
Short answer: why do we close temporary accounts at year-end?
sessions.analystNote: The accounting cycle is the foundation of every financial model. When your model 'closes' each period and retained earnings rolls forward, this is exactly what's happening.

sessions.title: Reading Annual Reports & IFRS Presentation Standards
learningObjectives: Describe the structure of a corporate annual report and what each section contains
Understand IAS 1 presentation requirements: fair presentation, going concern, accrual basis, materiality
Read and interpret a Statement of Financial Position (Balance Sheet) under IFRS — current/non-current classification
Read and interpret a Statement of Comprehensive Income: profit or loss + other comprehensive income
Understand the Statement of Changes in Equity and what moves through it
Identify key disclosure requirements: notes to accounts, accounting policies, contingencies
Calculate and interpret the current ratio from a real balance sheet
keyConcepts: IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements
Fair presentation and compliance with IFRS
Materiality: only material items need separate disclosure
Current vs. non-current classification on the balance sheet
Other Comprehensive Income (OCI): items that bypass the income statement
Notes to accounts: accounting policies, estimates, contingencies
Comparative information: two years presented side by side
coreFormulasForLibrary: Total Comprehensive Income = Profit or Loss + Other Comprehensive Income (OCI)
Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
quizTopics: Multiple choice: classify items as current vs. non-current on the balance sheet
Short answer: what is the difference between profit for the period and total comprehensive income?
Fill-in-the-blank: given line items, construct a simplified IFRS Statement of Financial Position
sessions.analystNote: When you receive a CIM (Confidential Information Memorandum) in PE, you'll be reading IFRS financial statements in exactly this format. Speed and accuracy in reading these is a core skill.

sessions.title: Internal Controls, Cash Management & Bank Reconciliation
learningObjectives: Define internal control and explain its five components (COSO framework: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information/communication, monitoring)
Describe the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) and its impact on internal controls
Explain the key cash control procedures: segregation of duties, authorization, reconciliation
Prepare a bank reconciliation: reconcile book balance to bank balance
Understand petty cash funds and their control
keyConcepts: Internal control: safeguard assets, ensure accurate records, promote efficiency, ensure compliance
Segregation of duties: authorization, custody, recordkeeping separated
Bank reconciliation: timing differences (outstanding checks, deposits in transit) vs. errors
Adjusted book balance = Adjusted bank balance (after reconciliation)
SOX Section 302 (CEO/CFO certification) and Section 404 (internal control report)
coreFormulasForLibrary: Bank Reconciliation: Bank Balance + Deposits in Transit − Outstanding Checks ± Bank Errors = Adjusted Bank Balance
Book Balance + Credit memos − Debit memos ± Book Errors = Adjusted Book Balance
Adjusted Bank Balance must equal Adjusted Book Balance
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: complete a bank reconciliation given bank statement and book balance data
Multiple choice: identify which internal control procedure is violated in a given scenario
Short answer: why is segregation of duties the most important internal control?
sessions.analystNote: Due diligence in PE heavily focuses on internal controls. Weak controls = restatement risk = valuation haircut. Know what good controls look like.

sessions.title: Accounts Receivable, Bad Debts & Notes Receivable
learningObjectives: Record sales on credit and account for accounts receivable
Apply the allowance method for uncollectible accounts (bad debt expense)
Calculate bad debt expense using the percentage-of-sales method and the aging-of-receivables method
Understand the direct write-off method and why IFRS prefers the allowance method
Account for notes receivable: recording, interest accrual, collection or dishonor
Calculate and interpret Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) / Receivables Turnover
keyConcepts: Accounts receivable: amounts owed by customers for goods/services delivered
Allowance for doubtful accounts (contra-asset): estimated uncollectibles
Bad debt expense: income statement charge for expected uncollectibles
Net realizable value of receivables = Gross AR − Allowance
Aging schedule: categorizes AR by how long overdue
Notes receivable: formal written promise to pay, earns interest
coreFormulasForLibrary: Net Realizable Value of AR = Gross Accounts Receivable − Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) = (Accounts Receivable / Revenue) × 365
Receivables Turnover = Revenue / Average Accounts Receivable
Interest on note = Principal × Annual Rate × (Time / 12 or Time / 365)
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: calculate allowance for doubtful accounts using an aging schedule
Multiple choice: what is the journal entry when a previously written-off account is collected?
Short answer: explain the difference between bad debt expense and the allowance for doubtful accounts
sessions.analystNote: DSO is a key working capital metric in PE due diligence. Rising DSO means customers are taking longer to pay — potential sign of revenue quality issues or customer financial stress.

sessions.title: Inventory Accounting: FIFO, Weighted Average & Lower of Cost
learningObjectives: Distinguish between a merchandising company and a service company; understand the cost of goods sold (COGS) calculation
Explain the two inventory systems: perpetual vs. periodic
Apply the three inventory costing methods under IFRS: FIFO and Weighted Average (LIFO not permitted under IFRS)
Calculate ending inventory and COGS under each method
Apply the lower of cost and net realizable value (LCNRV) rule for inventory write-downs
Calculate gross profit margin and inventory turnover
keyConcepts: COGS = Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory
Gross profit = Revenue − COGS
FIFO: first goods in are first goods out; ending inventory = most recent costs
Weighted average cost: total cost / total units
LCNRV: inventory written down if NRV < cost (IAS 2)
Inventory turnover: how many times inventory is sold and replaced per year
Days in inventory: average number of days to sell inventory
coreFormulasForLibrary: COGS = Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory
Gross Profit = Revenue − COGS
Gross Profit Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue × 100%
Inventory Turnover = COGS / Average Inventory
Days in Inventory = 365 / Inventory Turnover
Weighted Average Cost per unit = Total Cost of Goods Available / Total Units Available
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given purchase data, calculate ending inventory and COGS under FIFO and weighted average
Multiple choice: under IFRS, which inventory methods are permitted?
Short answer: how does choosing FIFO vs. weighted average affect the income statement and balance sheet in a period of rising prices?
sessions.analystNote: Gross margin analysis is the first thing analysts do with a company. Knowing how inventory method choice affects COGS (and thus margin) is a common interview topic.

sessions.title: Property, Plant & Equipment: Recognition, Depreciation & Disposal
learningObjectives: Apply the recognition criteria for PPE (IAS 16): probable future economic benefits, reliable measurement of cost
Determine the cost of PPE: purchase price + all costs to bring asset to working condition
Calculate depreciation using straight-line, units-of-production, and double-declining balance methods
Explain the concept of residual value and useful life
Record the disposal of PPE: calculate gain or loss on disposal
Understand the revaluation model as an alternative to cost model (IFRS only)
Account for impairment of PPE (IAS 36)
keyConcepts: PPE cost: purchase price + installation + delivery + legal fees to acquire
Straight-line depreciation: equal charge each year
Double-declining balance (DDB): accelerated depreciation front-loads charges
Units-of-production: depreciation based on actual usage
Carrying amount = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation
Gain/loss on disposal = Proceeds − Carrying Amount
Impairment: carrying amount > recoverable amount → write down
coreFormulasForLibrary: Straight-Line Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) / Useful Life
DDB Depreciation = Carrying Amount × (2 / Useful Life)
Units-of-Production Depreciation = (Cost − Residual Value) / Total Expected Units × Units Produced
Carrying Amount = Cost − Accumulated Depreciation
Gain or Loss on Disposal = Sale Proceeds − Carrying Amount at Disposal
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: calculate depreciation for 3 years under straight-line and DDB for a given asset
Multiple choice: what is the journal entry to record sale of equipment at a loss?
Short answer: explain how depreciation method choice affects operating income and tax in the early years of an asset's life
sessions.analystNote: D&A is added back to get EBITDA in every financial model. Understanding what drives D&A (useful life assumptions, method) is essential for building accurate projections.

sessions.title: Intangible Assets, R&D & Long-Term Asset Analysis
learningObjectives: Identify types of intangible assets: patents, trademarks, copyrights, franchises, goodwill
Distinguish finite-life intangibles (amortized) from indefinite-life intangibles (not amortized, tested for impairment)
Account for internally generated vs. acquired intangibles (IFRS: most internally generated not capitalized)
Understand IAS 38 rules for R&D: research phase expensed, development phase may be capitalized
Calculate and interpret the asset turnover ratio and return on assets (ROA)
keyConcepts: Goodwill: excess of purchase price over fair value of net identifiable assets; only arises on acquisition
Goodwill is not amortized under IFRS — tested annually for impairment
Finite-life intangibles: amortized over useful life (like PPE depreciation)
IAS 38: R&D — research expensed always; development capitalized if meets 6 criteria
Asset turnover = Revenue / Average Total Assets (efficiency metric)
Return on Assets (ROA) = Net Income / Average Total Assets
coreFormulasForLibrary: Goodwill = Acquisition Price − Fair Value of Net Identifiable Assets Acquired
Asset Turnover = Revenue / Average Total Assets
Return on Assets (ROA) = Net Income / Average Total Assets
Amortization of finite-life intangible = Cost / Useful Life (straight-line typical)
quizTopics: Multiple choice: under IAS 38, which R&D costs can be capitalized?
Short answer: company A acquires company B for €500m. B's net identifiable assets are worth €380m. Calculate goodwill.
Fill-in-the-blank: given an asset schedule, calculate total D&A and ending carrying values
sessions.analystNote: Goodwill is huge in M&A. When a PE fund acquires a company, almost all the premium over book value creates goodwill. Annual impairment testing can lead to write-downs that destroy earnings.

sessions.title: Financial Asset Classification & Intercorporate Investments
learningObjectives: Classify investments under IFRS 9: amortised cost, FVOCI, FVTPL (fair value through profit or loss)
Account for held-to-maturity (amortised cost) debt investments
Account for available-for-sale (FVOCI) equity investments: unrealized gains/losses go to OCI
Account for trading securities (FVTPL): unrealized gains/losses on income statement
Understand the equity method for significant influence investments (20–50% ownership)
Understand consolidation: when and why subsidiaries are consolidated (>50% control)
Explain goodwill and non-controlling interest in consolidated statements
Account for foreign currency transactions: transaction gains/losses on income statement
keyConcepts: IFRS 9 classification: based on business model and cash flow characteristics
Equity method: investor records share of investee's net income as investment income
Consolidation: parent + subsidiary presented as single economic entity
Non-controlling interest (NCI): the portion of equity not owned by parent
Goodwill on consolidation: purchase price minus fair value of net assets acquired
Foreign currency transaction risk: payables/receivables denominated in foreign currency
coreFormulasForLibrary: Equity Method: Investment income = Ownership % × Investee's Net Income
Equity Method: Investment carrying value = Cost + Share of Net Income − Dividends received
Consolidated Goodwill = Purchase Price − (Fair Value of Net Assets × Ownership%)
FX Transaction Gain/Loss = Change in exchange rate × Foreign currency amount
quizTopics: Multiple choice: company owns 30% of investee — which accounting method applies?
Short answer: explain the difference between the equity method and consolidation
Fill-in-the-blank: calculate equity method investment carrying value after one year
sessions.analystNote: Consolidation is directly relevant to M&A. When a company acquires >50%, it consolidates — understanding what goes on the balance sheet and where NCI sits is tested in every technical interview.

sessions.title: Current Liabilities & Bond Financing
learningObjectives: Identify and classify current liabilities: accounts payable, accrued liabilities, unearned revenues, short-term debt
Account for contingent liabilities under IAS 37: provision, disclosure, or ignore based on probability
Explain bonds payable: face value, coupon rate, market rate, issuance at par / discount / premium
Calculate issue price of a bond using present value concepts
Amortize bond discount/premium using the straight-line method and effective interest method
Record bond interest expense and carrying value over the life of the bond
keyConcepts: Current liabilities: due within one year or operating cycle
Contingent liability: record if probable and estimable; disclose if possible; ignore if remote
Bond payable: formal debt instrument with face value and periodic coupon payments
Bond issued at discount: market rate > coupon rate; carrying value < face value
Bond issued at premium: market rate < coupon rate; carrying value > face value
Effective interest method: interest expense = carrying value × market rate
coreFormulasForLibrary: Bond Issue Price = PV of coupons (annuity) + PV of face value (lump sum) at market rate
Interest Expense (effective method) = Carrying Value of Bond × Market Interest Rate
Carrying Value of Bond = Face Value − Unamortized Discount (or + Unamortized Premium)
Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) = (Accounts Payable / COGS) × 365
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: calculate bond carrying value and interest expense in year 1 (discount scenario)
Multiple choice: a bond with face value €1,000 and coupon 5% is issued when market rate is 6% — issued at par, discount, or premium?
Short answer: explain how issuing bonds at a discount affects the income statement vs. issuing at par
sessions.analystNote: Bonds and debt are the core of LBO financing. Understanding how interest expense is calculated, how carrying value moves, and what covenants attach to debt is critical for LBO modeling.

sessions.title: Leases, Long-Term Debt & Leverage Analysis
learningObjectives: Distinguish between finance leases and operating leases under IFRS 16
Understand that IFRS 16 brings most leases onto the balance sheet (right-of-use asset + lease liability)
Record finance lease: initial recognition, depreciation of ROU asset, interest on lease liability
Explain convertible bonds and notes: features and conversion accounting
Calculate and interpret key leverage ratios: debt-to-equity, debt-to-assets, interest coverage
Understand off-balance-sheet financing and why analysts adjust for it
keyConcepts: IFRS 16: all leases > 12 months → Right-of-Use asset + Lease Liability on balance sheet
Finance lease: front-loads expenses (interest + depreciation) vs. operating lease (straight-line rent)
Leverage: use of debt to amplify returns (and risk)
Interest coverage ratio: EBIT / Interest Expense — measures ability to service debt
Debt/EBITDA: most common leverage metric in leveraged finance and PE
coreFormulasForLibrary: Debt-to-Equity Ratio = Total Debt / Total Equity
Debt-to-Assets Ratio = Total Debt / Total Assets
Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT / Interest Expense (must be > 1.5–2x to be safe)
Net Debt = Total Debt − Cash and Cash Equivalents
Debt / EBITDA = Net Debt / EBITDA (key leverage metric in PE; typical LBO target: 4–6x)
quizTopics: Multiple choice: under IFRS 16, how does a 5-year lease affect the balance sheet at inception?
Short answer: a company has EBIT of €50m and interest expense of €20m. Is this coverage ratio concerning?
Fill-in-the-blank: calculate debt/equity and interest coverage from a given balance sheet and income statement
sessions.analystNote: Debt/EBITDA is the single most important leverage metric in PE. LBOs are typically structured at 4–6x Debt/EBITDA. Know this ratio cold and be able to calculate it from financial statements instantly.

sessions.title: Share Capital, Retained Earnings & Equity Transactions
learningObjectives: Understand the components of shareholders' equity: share capital (ordinary and preference), share premium, retained earnings, OCI reserves, treasury shares
Account for the issuance of ordinary shares at par and above par
Account for preference shares: cumulative vs. non-cumulative dividends
Record cash dividends and share dividends; explain their effect on equity
Account for share buybacks (treasury shares): cost method
Understand IPOs and why companies go public (relevant context: L'Occitane Hong Kong IPO)
Calculate earnings per share (EPS) — basic and diluted
Calculate return on equity (ROE) and explain the DuPont decomposition
keyConcepts: Authorised vs. issued vs. outstanding shares
Share premium: amount received above par value
Retained earnings: cumulative undistributed profits
Treasury shares: repurchased by the company — reduce equity (contra-equity)
Cash dividend: reduces both retained earnings and cash
Share dividend: transfers from retained earnings to share capital — no cash outflow
EPS = Net Income attributable to ordinary shareholders / Weighted Average Shares Outstanding
coreFormulasForLibrary: Basic EPS = Net Income (after preference dividends) / Weighted Average Ordinary Shares
Return on Equity (ROE) = Net Income / Average Shareholders' Equity
DuPont ROE = Net Profit Margin × Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier
Equity Multiplier = Total Assets / Total Equity (= 1 + Debt/Equity)
Book Value per Share = Total Shareholders' Equity / Shares Outstanding
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given share issuance and dividend data, reconstruct the statement of changes in equity
Multiple choice: how does a share buyback affect EPS?
Short answer: explain the DuPont decomposition of ROE and what each component tells you
sessions.analystNote: ROE and the DuPont breakdown are common interview topics. A company can have high ROE purely from leverage (equity multiplier) rather than operational excellence — analysts need to distinguish these drivers.

sessions.title: Statement of Cash Flows: Operating Activities
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of the cash flow statement and why it differs from the income statement
Distinguish the three sections: operating, investing, financing activities
Prepare the operating section using the indirect method: start with net income and adjust for non-cash items and working capital changes
Identify non-cash adjustments: add back D&A, add back impairments, adjust for gains/losses on asset sales
Understand working capital changes: increase in AR = use of cash; increase in AP = source of cash
Explain free cash flow (FCF) and why it matters more than net income to analysts
keyConcepts: Indirect method: Net Income → adjust for non-cash items → adjust for WC changes = Cash from Operations
D&A is added back (non-cash expense that reduced income but didn't use cash)
Gains on asset sales are subtracted (included in net income but cash inflow goes to investing section)
Increase in current assets (AR, inventory) = use of cash
Increase in current liabilities (AP, accrued liabilities) = source of cash
Free Cash Flow (FCF) = Cash from Operations − Capital Expenditures
coreFormulasForLibrary: Cash from Operations (indirect) = Net Income + D&A + Impairments − Gains on Sales ± Changes in Working Capital
Free Cash Flow (FCF) = Cash from Operations − Capital Expenditures (CapEx)
Change in Working Capital = Change in Current Assets − Change in Current Liabilities
Cash Conversion Cycle = DSO + Days in Inventory − DPO
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given an income statement and balance sheet changes, prepare the operating section of the cash flow statement using the indirect method
Multiple choice: depreciation expense increases — what is the effect on cash from operations?
Short answer: a company has net income of €100m but FCF of −€20m. What are three possible reasons?
sessions.analystNote: FCF is the foundation of DCF valuation. Every single valuation model you will ever build starts here. Mastering the cash flow statement is non-negotiable for any IB/PE analyst.

sessions.title: Investing & Financing Cash Flows + Full SCF Construction
learningObjectives: Identify cash flows from investing activities: purchase/sale of PPE, acquisitions, investments
Identify cash flows from financing activities: debt issuance/repayment, share issuance/buyback, dividends paid
Prepare a complete statement of cash flows from scratch using the indirect method
Reconcile beginning and ending cash: Operating + Investing + Financing = Change in Cash
Analyze a cash flow statement to assess quality of earnings and capital allocation decisions
Interpret cash flow patterns: growth vs. mature vs. distressed company profiles
keyConcepts: Investing outflows: CapEx, acquisitions, loans made to others
Investing inflows: proceeds from asset sales, acquisitions proceeds, loan repayments received
Financing inflows: new debt, share issuance
Financing outflows: debt repayment, share buybacks, dividends
Net change in cash = Operating + Investing + Financing
Quality of earnings: is operating cash flow consistently higher than net income?
coreFormulasForLibrary: Cash Flow Statement Equation: Cash from Operations + Cash from Investing + Cash from Financing = Net Change in Cash
Ending Cash = Beginning Cash + Net Change in Cash
CapEx (from SCF) = Ending PPE − Beginning PPE + Depreciation (or read directly from investing section)
Cash Return on Assets = Cash from Operations / Average Total Assets
quizTopics: Fill-in-the-blank: given all three sections' line items, complete a full cash flow statement and verify it reconciles
Multiple choice: a company has positive net income but large negative operating cash flow — what does this likely indicate?
Short answer: describe the cash flow profile you would expect from a high-growth tech startup vs. a mature utility company
sessions.analystNote: Being able to build the SCF from scratch (given only a P&L and two balance sheets) is a classic interview test in IB. Practice this until you can do it in under 10 minutes.

sessions.title: Ratio Analysis: Profitability, Efficiency & Liquidity
learningObjectives: Perform horizontal analysis (trend analysis) and vertical analysis (common-size statements)
Calculate and interpret profitability ratios: gross margin, operating margin, net margin, ROA, ROE
Calculate and interpret efficiency ratios: asset turnover, inventory turnover, receivables turnover, payables turnover
Calculate and interpret liquidity ratios: current ratio, quick ratio, cash ratio
Apply the DuPont framework to decompose ROE into its three drivers
keyConcepts: Horizontal analysis: % change year over year
Vertical analysis: each line as % of revenue (income statement) or total assets (balance sheet)
Gross margin = Gross Profit / Revenue
Operating margin = EBIT / Revenue
EBITDA margin = EBITDA / Revenue (most used in PE/IB)
Quick ratio = (Cash + Short-term investments + AR) / Current Liabilities
Cash Conversion Cycle = DSO + DIO − DPO
coreFormulasForLibrary: Gross Margin = Gross Profit / Revenue
EBITDA = Net Income + Interest + Taxes + Depreciation + Amortization
EBITDA Margin = EBITDA / Revenue
Operating Margin (EBIT Margin) = EBIT / Revenue
Quick Ratio = (Cash + Marketable Securities + Accounts Receivable) / Current Liabilities
Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) = DSO + Days Inventory Outstanding − DPO
